claims.claim: The U.S. Constitution is the supreme law of the United States; Article VI provides that the Constitution, the laws of the United States made in pursuance of it, and treaties are 'the supreme Law of the Land,' binding judges in every state.

The Constitution was drafted in Philadelphia in 1787 by delegates to the Constitutional Convention, was signed on September 17, 1787, and was ratified in 1788 when New Hampshire became the ninth state to approve it, meeting Article VII's requirement of nine of thirteen states.

The Constitution's structure is a Preamble, seven articles, and twenty-seven amendments: Article I creates the legislative branch, Article II the executive, Article III the judiciary, Article IV covers relations among the states, Article V the amendment process, Article VI supremacy and oaths, and Article VII ratification.
The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the Constitution; Congress proposed twelve amendments in 1789 and ten were ratified by three-fourths of the state legislatures on December 15, 1791.

Article V provides the amendment process: Congress proposes amendments by a two-thirds vote of both houses (or a convention called on application of two-thirds of the states), and an amendment becomes part of the Constitution when ratified by three-fourths of the states, either by their legislatures or by state conventions.

The Constitution has been amended twenty-seven times since ratification; the first ten amendments (the Bill of Rights) were added in 1791, and only seventeen amendments have been added since, reflecting how deliberately difficult the Article V process is.

The Preamble opens the Constitution with its stated purposes: to form a more perfect Union, establish Justice, insure domestic Tranquility, provide for the common defence, promote the general Welfare, and secure the Blessings of Liberty to ourselves and our Posterity.

How to interpret the Constitution's text is an open debate: the Library of Congress's Constitution Annotated documents how the Constitution has been interpreted over time through Supreme Court case law, while OpenStax's American Government calls the document a 'living document'; judges and scholars differ between reading the text by its original meaning and reading it as evolving with society.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How the Constitution's text should be interpreted — by its original meaning as understood at ratification, or as an evolving document whose meaning develops with society.
positions: Original-meaning reading: the Constitution's words should carry the meaning they had when ratified, limiting judges to that understanding.

Evolving interpretation: the Constitution's broad language is applied to circumstances the framers could not foresee, so its meaning develops through interpretation over time (the 'living document' view).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states both positions factually and attributes them: the Constitution Annotated exists precisely to record how the Constitution has been interpreted over time, and OpenStax's text uses 'living document' language. The lesson takes no side and leaves the question open, as the sources do.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Exactly when the Constitution took effect: it was signed September 17, 1787, but ratification took time.
positions: Ratified in 1788 — New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify in the summer of 1788, satisfying Article VII.
The new federal government began operating in 1789, when the first Congress convened.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the National Archives framing: the Constitution was drafted and signed in 1787 and ratified in 1788 (New Hampshire, the ninth state). The 1789 start of the new government is noted where relevant, but the working definition anchors on the 1788 ratification.

sourceRecords.title: Constitution of the United States (1787)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. National Archives and Records Administration
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: the Convention convened in the State House (Independence Hall) in Philadelphia on May 14, 1787, to revise the Articles of Confederation; the delegates decided by mid-June to draft an entirely new frame of government; the four-page document was drafted in secret during the summer of 1787 and signed on September 17, 1787. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: The Constitution Annotated (Constitution of the United States of America: Analysis and Interpretation)
sourceRecords.provider: Library of Congress / Congressional Research Service, via congress.gov
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. The live host is behind a bot challenge; read via Wayback captures of the canonical URL (20260601173713 homepage; 20191018235445 about page). The Constitution Annotated provides a legal analysis and interpretation of the Constitution based on a comprehensive review of Supreme Court case law and relevant historical practices, and its homepage describes it as a comprehensive overview of how the Constitution has been interpreted over time. Supports the authoritative-source framing and the living-text debate's attributed documentation of interpretation over time.

Facts synthesized in original prose.
